items.prose: A symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix has eigenvalue 6 along $(1, 1)$ and eigenvalue $t$ along $(1, -1)$.
items.question: Write its off-diagonal entry as an expression in $t$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the matrix as $6\,\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + t\,\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T$ with unit vectors.

byKey.no-half: You left out the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from the unit vectors $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, \pm 1)$.
byKey.diagonal: That is the diagonal entry. Off the diagonal the second piece subtracts.
byKey.swap: You took the pieces the wrong way round. The 6 goes with $(1, 1)$, whose piece is all $+\tfrac{1}{2}$.

explain.text: The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}3 + \tfrac{t}{2} & 3 - \tfrac{t}{2}\\ 3 - \tfrac{t}{2} & 3 + \tfrac{t}{2}\end{pmatrix}$. Check at $t = 6$: the off-diagonal is 0 and the matrix is $6\mathbf{I}$, as it must be.

items.prose: Prove that a real symmetric $\mathbf{A}$ has only real eigenvalues. Write $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ for the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{x}$; note $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x} = \sum_i |x_i|^2$.
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: Let $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$, where $\lambda$ and $\mathbf{x}$ may be complex

feedback.correct: The number $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ equals both $\lambda$ and $\bar{\lambda}$ times a positive number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ two ways, then compare.

byKey.conj: The conjugate eigenvalue appears only after $\mathbf{A}$ has moved onto $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$. Put the symmetry line first.
byKey.conclude: The positivity of $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x}$ is used last, to cancel it from the subtracted line.

explain.text: We computed $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ twice: once as $\lambda\,\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x}$, once as $\bar{\lambda}\,\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x}$ using symmetry and realness. Since $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x} > 0$, $\lambda = \bar{\lambda}$. A rotation such as $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric, and its eigenvalues are $\pm i$.

items.question: Above what value of $t$ is $\mathbf{A}$ positive definite? Give 3 decimal places.

widget.label: Threshold for t
widget.accept: $2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828$: all three determinants are positive exactly when $t > 2\sqrt{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make each leading determinant positive and keep the strictest condition.

byKey.two-by-two: You stopped at the $2 \times 2$ condition, $t > 2$. The $3 \times 3$ needs $t(t^2 - 8) > 0$, so $t > 2\sqrt{2}$.
byKey.zero: $t > 0$ is only the first condition. The bigger corners demand more.
byKey.eight: You solved $t^2 > 8$ as $t > 8$. Take the square root: $t > 2\sqrt{2}$.

explain.text: With $t > 0$, $t^3 - 8t = t(t^2 - 8) > 0$ needs $t^2 > 8$, which also covers $t^2 > 4$. So the threshold is $2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828$. The eigenvalues are $t$ and $t \pm 2\sqrt{2}$, and the smallest hits 0 exactly there.

items.prose: Over three days, A returned $2\%$, $-1\%$, $2\%$ and B returned $1\%$, $0\%$, $-4\%$. Divide by $n = 3$ throughout.
items.question: Fill in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, then the variance of the portfolio $(1, 1)$ computed straight from its return series.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Demean each stock (means 1 and $-1$), then average the squares and products.

byKey.r3c1: The portfolio returned $3, -1, -2$ with mean 0, so its variance is $\tfrac{1}{3}(9 + 1 + 4) = \tfrac{14}{3}$.

explain.text: Demeaned, A is $(1, -2, 1)$ and B is $(2, 1, -3)$, giving $\sigma_A^2 = 2$, $\sigma_B^2 = \tfrac{14}{3}$ and $\sigma_{AB} = -1$. Then $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = 2 + \tfrac{14}{3} - 2 = \tfrac{14}{3}$. The series $3, -1, -2$ gives the same $\tfrac{14}{3}$ directly.

items.prose: Two returns have $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$, in $\%^2$, with eigenvalue 9 along $(1, 1)$ and 1 along $(1, -1)$.
items.question: How long is the long half-axis of the ellipse $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = 4$, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac{1}{9}$ and 1; the half-axes are $\sqrt{c/\lambda}$ for those.

byKey.sigma-not-inverse: You used $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$'s eigenvalue in $\sqrt{c/\lambda}$. The form uses $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, whose eigenvalue is $\tfrac{1}{9}$.
byKey.variance: You forgot the square root: $4 \times 9 = 36$ is a squared length.
byKey.no-c: That is the half-axis at level 1. At level 4 multiply by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.

explain.text: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac{1}{9}$ along $(1, 1)$ and 1 along $(1, -1)$. Half-axes are $\sqrt{4 \times 9} = 6$ and $\sqrt{4 \times 1} = 2$. The level 4 means two standard deviations along each axis.

items.prose: You hedge a position with $h_1, h_2$ units of two futures. The leftover variance, in $\%^2$, is $V(\mathbf{h}) = 9 - 2\mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{h}^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{h}$ with $\mathbf{c} = (3, 2)$ and $\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix}4&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. $\mathbf{S}$ is positive definite, so $V$ is a bowl with one lowest point.
items.question: What is the smallest leftover variance? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the gradient $2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{h} - 2\mathbf{c}$ to zero, solve for $\mathbf{h}$, then evaluate $V$.

byKey.unhedged: That is the variance with no hedge. The bowl's lowest point is lower.
byKey.value-h: That is $h_1 = \tfrac{4}{7}$, the hedge itself. The question asks for the variance left over.

explain.text: The gradient is $2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{h} - 2\mathbf{c}$, zero at $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{c} = \tfrac{1}{7}(4, 5)$. Then $V = 9 - \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{h} = 9 - \tfrac{12 + 10}{7} = \tfrac{41}{7} \approx 5.857$. The Hessian $2\mathbf{S}$ is positive definite, so this is the unique minimum.

items.title: One covariance matrix, read four ways
items.prompt:
Two stocks have daily covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$, in $\%^2$.

1. Show $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is positive definite by two different tests.
2. Find its eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors. Write $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$ and check it as a sum of rank-one pieces.
3. Among portfolios with $|\mathbf{w}| = 1$, which has the least variance, and what is it? Justify.
4. Give the directions and lengths of the half-axes of the risk ellipse $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = 1$.
5. A trader calls $\mathbf{w} = (1, -2)$ a riskless hedge. Compute its variance and comment.
items.model:
**1. Positive definite.** Leading determinants: $5 > 0$ and $5 \times 2 - 2^2 = 6 > 0$. Pivots: 5, then $2 - \tfrac{2}{5} \times 2 = \tfrac{6}{5} > 0$. Either test shows a bowl.

**2. Eigen-decomposition.** $\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = (5 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 1)$, so $\lambda_1 = 6$, $\lambda_2 = 1$. For 6: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} - 6\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\2&-4\end{pmatrix}$, so $(2, 1)$. For 1: $\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $(1, -2)$. They are perpendicular, $2 - 2 = 0$, as the spectral theorem promises. Normalise: $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2, 1)$, $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1, -2)$.

$$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T, \quad \mathbf{Q} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$$

Check: $6 \cdot \tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix} + 1 \cdot \tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}25&10\\10&10\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$.

**3. Least variance.** Write $\mathbf{w} = c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$ with $c_1^2 + c_2^2 = 1$. Then $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = 6c_1^2 + c_2^2 = 1 + 5c_1^2 \ge 1$, with equality at $c_1 = 0$. So $\mathbf{w} = \pm\mathbf{q}_2 = \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1, -2)$, with variance 1, a daily volatility of $1\%$.

**4. Risk ellipse.** $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ has the same eigenvectors with eigenvalues $\tfrac{1}{6}$ and 1. The half-axes are $1/\sqrt{1/6} = \sqrt{6} \approx 2.45$ along $(2, 1)$ and $1/\sqrt{1} = 1$ along $(1, -2)$. The long axis follows the larger variance.

**5. The trader's hedge.** $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = 5(1)^2 + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot (1)(-2) + 2(-2)^2 = 5 - 8 + 8 = 5$. Equivalently $\mathbf{w} = \sqrt{5}\,\mathbf{q}_2$, so the variance is $5 \times 1 = 5$, a volatility of about $2.24\%$. It is the least risky direction, but not riskless. Zero variance would need an eigenvalue of 0, and both are positive.

rubric.text: Applies two valid tests (leading determinants 5 and 6, pivots 5 and $\tfrac{6}{5}$, or eigenvalues) with correct numbers.
Finds eigenvalues 6 and 1 and eigenvectors along $(2, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$, normalised.
Writes $\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$ correctly and checks the sum of rank-one pieces returns $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
Identifies $\pm\mathbf{q}_2$ with variance 1, justified by $6c_1^2 + c_2^2$ or an equivalent argument.
Computes variance 5 for $(1, -2)$ and explains why it is not riskless.

items.question: What is the entry in row 1, column 2 of $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$? Give 3 decimal places.

widget.label: Row 1, column 2 of the inverse
widget.accept: $-\tfrac{2}{3}$: $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$, so it is row 2, column 1 of $\mathbf{Q}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Orthonormal columns give $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$; no elimination needed.

byKey.copied: You copied row 1, column 2 of $\mathbf{Q}$. The inverse is the transpose: read row 2, column 1.
byKey.recip: You inverted an entry, $1/(-\tfrac{2}{3})$. A matrix inverse is not entry by entry.

explain.text: Each column has length 1, for example $\tfrac{1}{9}(4 + 4 + 1) = 1$, and the columns are perpendicular. So $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$. Its row 1, column 2 entry is $Q_{21} = -\tfrac{2}{3}$.

items.prose: A risk model estimates $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ for 60 stocks from 40 days of returns, demeaning each stock first.
items.question: At least how many eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ are 0?

widget.label: Zero eigenvalues, at least
widget.accept: 21: rank at most $40 - 1 = 39$, so at least $60 - 39 = 21$ zero eigenvalues.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the largest possible rank, then subtract from 60.

byKey.no-demean: You used rank 40. Demeaning makes the 40 rows sum to zero, so the rank is at most 39.
byKey.rank: That is the largest possible rank. The zero eigenvalues are the rest of the 60.
byKey.days: You counted the days. Subtract the largest rank, 39, from the 60 stocks.

explain.text: The demeaned $40 \times 60$ matrix $\mathbf{R}$ has rows summing to zero, so its rank is at most 39. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is $60 \times 60$ with the same rank, leaving at least 21 zero eigenvalues: 21 directions of portfolios with zero sample variance.
